title: A datacenter the world can live with
intro: Every requirement below is drawn from a practice or a rule that exists somewhere in this ledger, with the document that shows it. Eight are met somewhere by a site or a binding rule; three are met only in part; one, assured hardware reuse, is not yet met anywhere in the record. The standard is the sum of practices that exist today, assembled in one place so that any site can be measured as a distance from it. Where a requirement is met by a rule rather than a site, the rule is cited; where the record shows the practice but not yet the measured result, that is said; where a proof rests on a press report of the document, the entry is marked.
how_to_read: Each requirement names what to ask for, what counts as proof, and which entries in the ledger show it being done. 'Proof' means a document someone outside the operator produced or assured; an entry listed under a requirement that rests on press reports or company statements is marked 'partly verified' or 'primary not found'.

requirements.title: Disclose site-level power and water, metered, every year
requirements.ask: Annual metered electricity (MWh) and water withdrawal, consumption and discharge (m³) for each site, published by the operator and reported to a public register.
requirements.proof: A statutory register or a settlement that binds future disclosure. A sustainability report alone is a claim.
requirements.note: The EU register exists, but per-site data sit behind an operator login and only an aggregate report is public; only 36% of in-scope sites reported in the first period. Germany's law requires reporting to a national register. At The Dalles, a settlement between the city and a newspaper released ten years of Google's annual water use and commits the city to disclose future annual figures on request ([press]; the settlement text was not read). The rule is written; public site-level disclosure is not yet practice anywhere in the ledger.

requirements.title: No drinking water for cooling where water is scarce; closed-loop or air cooling by default
requirements.ask: Cooling design stated in the permit, with the water source and the basin's status. In a stressed basin, air or closed-loop cooling. Where water is plentiful, seawater or reuse water before potable.
requirements.proof: The environmental assessment or permit naming the cooling system and the daily volume; a utility stating the connection is for office use only.
requirements.note: Uruguay's redesign states 48 m³ a day for one air-cooled building, against 7,600 m³ a day of potable water in the original two-building design (revised EIA, as reported in press). Amsterdam's siting policy prohibits groundwater extraction. Noord-Holland's provincial strategy records that its water company in practice now connects datacenters for office use only. Google is reported (by DCD) to say Hamina cools with seawater. In Chile an environmental tribunal partly annulled, as reported, the approval of a groundwater-cooled design; Google says it moved to an air-cooled design, which the environmental assessment service cleared in October 2026 without a new assessment (as reported by El Desconcierto; the resolution itself was not found).

requirements.title: Waste heat goes into a heat network, and the delivered figure is published
requirements.ask: Connection to a district heating system where one exists or can be built, with delivered MWh published by the network operator. Where no network exists, a cost-benefit analysis on the public record explaining why.
requirements.proof: The heat utility's annual report or a public body's case study giving delivered MWh; a statute requiring the analysis.
requirements.note: Stockholm's half-municipal utility reports, in its statutory accounts, 117 GWh of heat recovered in 2023 from Stockholm Data Parks and other Öppen Fjärrvärme sources combined. SEAI publishes cumulative MWh and tonnes for Tallaght's council-owned network. Denmark requires datacenters above 1 MW that are built or substantially renovated to analyse surplus heat and use it unless infeasible; Germany sets 10% reuse for sites commissioned from July 2026, rising to 20%. Across the EU, the sites that reported in the first period (about 36% of those in scope) reused about 1.8% of their heat, so the gap between the rule and the practice is the distance to close.

requirements.title: Firm, additional, clean supply, or bring your own
requirements.ask: Electricity from a contracted firm clean source named in a regulator-approved agreement, preferably one that would not otherwise have been built (geothermal, a hydro allocation), or the obligation to bring dispatchable supply before connecting. Existing nuclear contracted front-of-meter, so that the load pays grid charges, is firm and clean but not additional. Annual renewable certificates do not meet this.
requirements.proof: A regulator-approved tariff or supply agreement naming the resource; a connection policy that requires it.
requirements.note: Québec requires ministerial authorisation for projects of 5 MW or more, scored partly on heat recovery (per a law firm's summary); its proposed datacenter tariff awaits the Régie. Per a law firm's summary, Ireland requires new sites of 10 MVA or more to bring dispatchable capacity equal to their import, and sites from 1 MVA to source 80% from additional Irish renewables over six years. Talen states that Amazon contracts up to 1,920 MW from the existing Susquehanna plant, moving front-of-meter after FERC's rejection; no record of that or of grid charges paid was found yet. In Nevada, NV Energy's compliance filings cite the regulator's order of 11 March 2025 on a Clean Transition Tariff reached through a settlement, whose filed terms are meant to keep costs off other customers, and an order of 14 May 2025 on Google's 115 MW geothermal supply agreement (the orders themselves have not been read). Kenya's EcoCloud geothermal tariff and Teraco's wheeled solar rest on press and company statements. None of these has hourly matching verified by a third party on the public record; that is the next bar.

requirements.title: No new fossil generation built for the site, and no unpermitted generation ever
requirements.ask: The interconnection and utility filings show the load is served without a new gas plant built for it. On-site generators are permitted before they run, sized and listed in the air permit.
requirements.proof: The grid operator's queue and the utility commission's order; the air permit with generator count and capacity.
requirements.note: Ireland's planning board refused a datacenter, among other reasons because without a grid agreement on-site gas could become its primary supply, contrary to the government's statement that 'islanded' datacenters are not in line with national policy. The counter-examples in the ledger (a 944 MW peaker approved in Virginia, turbines run in Memphis for about a year before the first permit, 4,678 MW of gas permitted but not yet built in Pennsylvania) are what this requirement is measured against. Ireland's connection policy requires new sites to bring dispatchable on-site capacity without prescribing the fuel, so it is listed under supply, not here.

requirements.title: The site pays for the grid it needs
requirements.ask: Large loads pay for the transmission and generation built to serve them, with a minimum-take obligation and a long contract, so that residential bills do not carry the cost.
requirements.proof: A utility commission order setting the tariff; an auditor's or market monitor's finding of the bill effect.
requirements.note: Virginia's regulator, in its November 2025 order in Dominion's biennial review (PUR-2025-00058), created a rate class (GS-5, from 1 January 2027) for customers of 25 MW or more at a load factor of at least 75%, with 14-year contracts and minimum demand charges of 85% for distribution, 85% for transmission and 60% for generation. Ohio's regulator approved a datacenter tariff in July 2025: per the utility's tariff page and the state consumer counsel, loads above 25 MW pay for up to 85% of subscribed capacity after a ramp, on contracts of up to 12 years (a ramp of up to four years plus eight); the order is under appeal at the Ohio Supreme Court. Wisconsin's regulator, in May 2026 (docket 6630-TE-113), made a large-customer tariff mandatory for loads of 100 MW or more, with 15-year initial terms. Ontario's Bill 40 lets regulations restrict large-load connections, and a proposed framework would put new datacenters in a separate rate class; Hydro-Québec has proposed a datacenter tariff that awaits the Régie. The PJM market monitor's counterfactual estimate ($16.6 billion of capacity-auction revenue across two auctions attributable to datacenter load) and Virginia's legislative auditor's projection ($14–37 a month on a typical residential bill by 2040 under unconstrained demand) are estimates of what is at stake without such rules.

requirements.title: Land take is accounted for and biodiversity is a condition, not a brochure
requirements.ask: Hectares taken and previous land use stated in the application; a biodiversity condition with a metric, a monitoring duty and an enforcement body; siting rules that keep hyperscale off farmland and out of green belts unless a public body decides otherwise in writing.
requirements.proof: A planning decision with the condition in it; a national siting rule.
requirements.note: England's Secretary of State imposed an enforceable 135% biodiversity net gain condition. The Netherlands confined new hyperscale datacenters to two named areas by national rule (draft approved June 2022; in force 1 January 2024, Stb. 2023, 492). That rule did not apply to Zeewolde, whose zoning plan was already adopted; there the state declined to sell the land the project needed, and Meta cancelled the campus in July 2022. Monitoring data from the English site does not exist yet because it is not built; the condition is the proof, the result is pending.

requirements.title: Noise is measured by a third party, before and after, and the results are public
requirements.ask: A baseline sound study before construction, a post-construction study, and annual studies for five years, all by an independent firm, with a design requirement that site noise not exceed ambient; a limit that addresses low-frequency tonal noise, which dBA does not capture.
requirements.proof: The ordinance or planning condition; the published studies.
requirements.note: Chandler, Arizona wrote baseline, post-construction and five annual third-party studies into its ordinance; no city-published results were found. Loudoun County reports that complaints often involve tonal noise, and states that it has no rule specific to tonal or low-frequency noise; amendments are anticipated in 2027. This requirement is met in part.

requirements.title: Public money buys audited jobs, with a clawback
requirements.ask: Any tax exemption or subsidy names the permanent on-site jobs and wages required, is evaluated by an independent auditor on a schedule, and is clawed back if the terms are not met.
requirements.proof: The incentive agreement; the auditor's evaluation.
requirements.note: Georgia and Virginia evaluate their exemptions by statute. Georgia's evaluation attributes 30% of datacenter activity to the exemption; its audit office first summarised job figures for all datacenter activity, then reissued them at 30% with no stated reason. No programme in the ledger ties the money to a jobs floor with a clawback: Uttar Pradesh's 2026 policy and Brazil's Redata regime set none. This requirement is met only in its first half: the evaluation exists; the condition does not.

requirements.title: Hardware lives as long as it can, and the reuse figure is assured
requirements.ask: Stated hardware lifespans, a reuse and recovery rate for servers and components, and the mineral sourcing for cobalt, nickel and rare earths traced to the mine, all within a third-party assurance scope.
requirements.proof: An assurance statement whose scope names the figure.
requirements.note: Microsoft publishes a 90.9% reuse-and-recycling rate for cloud servers and components, with a method; its third-party review covers waste tonnage, not that rate. Companies state accounting lives for servers (five to six years) in their filings; none found states a physical life for GPUs. No company in the ledger has an assured hardware reuse figure, and statutory conflict-minerals filings do not cover cobalt, nickel or rare earths. No site or rule in the ledger meets this requirement yet.

requirements.title: The grid operator publishes a reconciled datacenter forecast
requirements.ask: Queued, contracted and actually connected datacenter load published separately and reconciled, so that planning is not done against announcements.
requirements.proof: The grid operator's own forecast document.
requirements.note: Australia's AEMO publishes a project-reconciled forecast showing 67 GW in development, 27% connection utilisation and a 36% cancellation rate. RTE publishes, for the Paris region, connected datacenter capacity separately from capacity in the connection process and under study. Spain's grid operator publishes granted demand access by type and how much of it is in service. Texas, by contrast, publishes no file of its large-load queue (about 474 GW of requests in June 2026, per ERCOT testimony).

requirements.title: The mines and fabs behind the hardware move off inland water
requirements.ask: Copper, lithium and chip fabrication report water by source, with inland withdrawal falling and seawater or reuse rising, in regulator-published figures.
requirements.proof: The mining or water regulator's data, not the company's report.
requirements.note: Chile's copper commission records inland water use by copper mining falling from 12.0 to 10.8 m³/s between 2023 and 2024, and projects 7.6 m³/s by 2034 as desalination grows to about two thirds of supply. Chile's environmental regulator has capped SQM's brine and freshwater extraction at the Salar de Atacama under a compliance programme. That is two minerals in one country; there is no equivalent regulator figure for nickel in Indonesia or rare earths in Myanmar, and TSMC's own reports show its unit water use above its 2010 baseline.

closing: Twelve requirements. Eight are met somewhere; three (site-level disclosure, noise results, jobs clawbacks) only in part; one (assured hardware reuse) nowhere yet. None is met everywhere. A site that meets all twelve does not exist yet.
